for any aws user to be familiar with and
in this video i wanted to do a brief
overview of the service including some
of the key concepts that you should be
aware of afterwards we're going to head
over into the aws console and do a
hands-on demonstration of some of these
concepts in action so the first thing
that i wanted to do to describe how
cloudtrail is used in the aws ecosystem
is through a practical example so let's
assume that we have an aws account and
we want to interact with the dynamodb
service here now generally there's two
different actors that interact with aws
services either you the individual or
applications you develop but let's keep
this simple for now and just assume that
it's an individual performing actions on
a dynamodb table now there's many
different apis that you can utilize when
interacting with dynamodb when you're
initially interacting with it you may do
things like creating a table modifying
some of its properties and configuration
settings things like that these are
generally less common events we consider
them to be kind of administration or
control style events on your aws
resources and the second type of events
are kind of more granular type of events
so if you're querying a table you're
modifying some of the items you're
deleting some of the items these are
much more plentiful events especially if
you build an application that has a lot
of requests per second now what
cloudtrail is concerned with is
capturing and storing these events on
your aws account so there's two
categories here like i kind of described
the first category is management style
of events these are the control plane
events that indicate what you created
what you modified what you updated
against an aws service and then of
course there's more granular events and
we call these data events obviously much
more plentiful and much more chatty now
there's also a third category events
which i don't have for you in front of
the screen here but i wanted to mention
briefly and these are cloudtrail
insights now insights analyze your
management and data events to try to
identify anomalies and raise them to you
as a user from there you can alarm on
these types of events or set up
dashboards to keep an eye on them to
identify any anomalous behavior so
that's generally where cloudtrail fits
in so now let's take a look at
cloudtrail a little bit more closely so
first of all what is cloudtrail you
probably have an idea of where it fits
in at this point but it's an aws service
that allows for auditing security
monitoring and troubleshooting access to
aws services and like i mentioned
there's three different types of events
to be concerned with the first is
management style events the second is
data and the third is insights now the
core concept in cloudtrail is something
called trails and trails are collections
of instances of these types of events so
you can set up a trail for management
style events set up your own retention
policy and the particular types of
events that you want to capture you can
do something similar for data events so
you can say i'm only interested in
capturing dynamodb operations against my
service and you can create a trail just
for that and have a separate retention
policy for it so that's the idea you're
generally creating trails in your aws
account to capture these different types
of events now from there you may want to
store your events for longer periods of
time so with trails you can deliver your
events to cloudwatch or s3 for further
analysis so once your data is in
something like s3 you can hook it up to
something like amazon athena and then
use that to perform sql style queries
against your log files another option is
to integrate with cloudwatch which can
be a little bit more expensive but has
other benefits as well now optionally if
you don't want to deliver your events to
a custom storage solution you can
integrate with a relatively new feature
that cloudtrail released earlier this
year which is cloudtrail lake now this
feature allows you to keep all the
storage of these cloudtrail events
within the cloudtrail service and not
have to worry about integrating the
delivery with cloudwatch or s3 or other
aws services essentially it's a way for
you to keep all these events in one spot
within the cloudtrail service it does
cost a little bit more to do this but it
can be convenient for some use cases now
an important thing to note is that with
cloudtrail you get 90 days worth of
management events available for free in
the aws console now this comes activated
on every aws account that gets created
you don't need to toggle this on now as
a quick example of what you can expect
with management events here's a quick
little screenshot i pulled up of my
cloudtrail management dashboard so you
can see here there's many different
events that you can take a look at
over here on the left hand side the
leftmost column is the event name so you
can see this was a s3 service i was
interacting with down here described
table this was related to dynamodb you
can see things like the event time the
username that performed the action what
the event source was or the service that
was being accessed in this case and then
what resource was being accessed as well
and then over at the top it allows you
to apply certain filters and certain
time ranges that you may want to filter
down your data on now from here you can
also download these events to your local
machine in csv format or export this
data into something like athena for more
comprehensive analysis but this is
generally the idea of what you can
expect with cloudtrail from a user
perspective so now i want to talk about
some of the use cases that cloudtrail
helps address so one of the more common
ones is to identify the source ips of
requests and whether or not mfa was
enabled now these are just two very
simple examples but if you think about
any application you generally want to
log the ip addresses of applications or
users that are making requests to your
service from there you can analyze
things like top talkers by ip so this
can help you identify bad actors that
are potentially abusing a certain api or
a certain application flow and then have
a way to blacklist them if you need now
another cool feature is that you get
access to access denied errors so this
will help you identify when you have
compromised credentials so maybe you
have a user that accidentally published
their credentials to github and someone
captured that and they're trying to
access it and receiving all these errors
from there you can set up alarms on
these access denied errors so you can
identify which credentials are
compromised so that you can quickly
address it and the fourth one that is
particularly useful in my experience is
that many times you can use cloudtrail
to gather more verbose error logs when
an api call fails this is particularly
useful for those of you that are using
cloud formation often when you're
working with cloudformation which is an
infrastructure as code service you get
these very vague and ambiguous error
messages and it's often very very
difficult to debug exactly where your
application deployment went wrong so
using cloudtrail you have access to the
very specific error message that the aws
service emitted and not these general
vague ambiguous error messages so very
very useful from that perspective and in
other aws services say for example
you're trying to invoke dynamodb and you
get an error it can give you more
granular metadata about what went wrong
in your invocation as well so very very
handy and very useful to be aware of and
then finally you're able to group all
the events or all the trails from
multiple different ews accounts for
long-term auditing and storage now many
organizations may have security
requirements where they need to retain
their log files for longer periods of
time so cloudtrail helps you capture and
deliver those log files to multiple
different aws services so that you can
keep them around in cold storage so
these are some of the use cases that
cloudtrail can help you address i wanted
